n: Solomon resolves to build two houses: a temple for the Lord’s name and a royal palace. The temple comes first in his heart and in the Chronicler’s story.

f.g: God’s ‘name’ stands for His presence, authority, and character dwelling among His people.

n: Solomon organizes a huge labor force: 70,000 carriers, 80,000 stonecutters in the hills, and 3,600 supervisors.

f.g: Counted out or assigned.
Seventy thousand (a score = 20).

n: Solomon writes to Huram (also called Hiram), king of the Phoenician port of Tyre, asking for the same help he had given David in building his palace.

f.g: Spelled Hiram in Kings; Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician sea-trading city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

n: Solomon explains the temple’s purpose: a place dedicated to God for incense, the bread of the Presence, and daily, weekly, monthly, and festival sacrifices — a lasting pattern of worship.

f.g: Symbol of prayer rising to God.
The first day of each month, marked by special offerings.

n: The temple must be great because Israel’s God is greater than all the so-called gods of the nations.

f.w: great is our God above all gods

n: Solomon humbly admits that no building could contain God, whom even the highest heavens cannot hold. The temple is a place to meet and worship Him, not to box Him in.

f.w: heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him

n: Solomon asks for a master craftsman skilled in metals, dyed fabrics, and engraving to work alongside the artisans David had already gathered.

f.g: Skillful (the KJV meaning, without any sense of trickery).
To engrave or carve.
Expensive dyed threads, like those used in the tabernacle; Tyre was famous for purple dye.

n: He also requests cedar, cypress, and algum wood from Lebanon, acknowledging that Tyre’s woodsmen are the experts. His own workers will work beside them.

f.g: A prized, uncertain wood (perhaps red sandalwood or juniper), called almug in Kings.
Probably cypress or juniper.

n: Solomon needs a great amount of timber because the temple is to be “wonderful great” — astonishingly magnificent.

f.g: Extraordinarily great; marvelous.

n: In payment Solomon offers large amounts of wheat, barley, wine, and olive oil for Huram’s workers — Israel’s farm produce in exchange for Phoenicia’s timber.

f.g: Hebrew kor, a dry measure of roughly 6 bushels (about 220 liters).
A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).

n: Huram replies in writing with a gracious compliment: Solomon’s kingship is evidence of the Lord’s love for His people.

f.w: Because the LORD hath loved his people

n: Remarkably, this foreign king blesses Israel’s God as the Creator of heaven and earth and praises Him for giving David a wise son.

f.g: Endowed with good sense and insight.

n: Huram sends a skilled, gifted craftsman — also named Huram (Huram-abi). “Of Huram my father’s” is probably a title like “my master craftsman.”

f.g: Hebrew Huram-abi; ‘abi’ (my father) may be an honorific meaning master or counselor.

n: This craftsman had an Israelite mother from Dan and a Tyrian father. He was skilled in nearly every material and could design whatever was asked of him — like Bezaleel and Aholiab of old.

f.g: 1 Kings 7:14 says his mother was from Naphtali; perhaps her family had ties to both tribes.
Work out any design given to him.

n: Huram agrees to the payment Solomon offered and asks that it be sent.

f.g: A polite, deferential way of addressing Solomon.

n: Tyre’s workers would cut the logs, bind them into rafts, and float them down the coast to Joppa, Israel’s port, from which Solomon’s men would haul them up to Jerusalem.

f.g: Rafts of logs tied together.
Modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv — the same port Jonah sailed from.

n: Solomon takes a census of foreigners living in Israel — descendants of the earlier Canaanite peoples — following David’s earlier count. They number 153,600.

f.g: Non-Israelite residents of the land.

n: These resident foreigners are assigned as carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. The verse repeats the figures from verse 2, framing the chapter.

f.w: to set the people a work
f.g: To keep the people working; to supervise them.
